questions.answer: (i) RENEWABLE — can be renewed by natural processes; e.g. solar energy, wind, water, forests, wildlife. (ii) NON-RENEWABLE — take millions of years to form; e.g. coal, petroleum, most metallic minerals. Some renewables (sunlight) are continuous; others (forests) take time to replace.

questions.question: What is the difference between STOCK and RESERVES? Give one example of each.
questions.answer: STOCK is the material in the environment that can satisfy human needs but humans do not have the appropriate technology to use it (e.g. hydrogen as a clean fuel). RESERVES are a SUBSET of stock that can be put into use with present technology, but whose use has been postponed for the future (e.g. water in dams, mineral deposits left for later).
questions.explanation: Stock — tech missing; reserves — tech ready, use postponed.

questions.question: What is sustainable development? What was Agenda 21?
questions.answer: SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT means development that takes place without damaging the environment, and that does not compromise the needs of future generations. AGENDA 21 is a global declaration signed at the UNCED Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 — a global plan of action to combat environmental damage, poverty and disease through global cooperation. Every local government is expected to draw its own LOCAL AGENDA 21.

questions.question: What are the THREE steps of resource planning in India?
questions.answer: (i) Identification and inventory of resources across regions — through SURVEYING, MAPPING and qualitative-quantitative ESTIMATION. (ii) Evolving a PLANNING STRUCTURE with appropriate technology, skill and institutional set-up to implement resource development plans. (iii) MATCHING the resource development plans with overall NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT plans.

questions.question: Name three causes of land degradation in India and give one regional example for each.
questions.answer: (i) DEFORESTATION DUE TO MINING — Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha. (ii) OVER-GRAZING — Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh. (iii) OVER-IRRIGATION leading to water-logging and salinity — Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh. (Also: industrial effluents → land and water pollution.)

questions.question: Compare BLACK soil and LATERITE soil — region, formation, fertility, suitable crops.
questions.answer: BLACK SOIL — found in the Deccan trap (Maharashtra, MP, Saurashtra, Malwa, Chhattisgarh) on basalt lava flows; rich in calcium, magnesium, potash and lime; holds moisture; ideal for COTTON, also pulses and millets. LATERITE SOIL — found in areas of high temperature and high rainfall (Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, MP, Odisha, Assam hills); formed by intense leaching that removes lime and silica, leaving iron and aluminium; LOW humus; needs manures + fertilisers; suitable for tea, coffee, cashew nut.

questions.question: Explain different methods of soil conservation. Discuss with at least four examples.
questions.answer: (i) CONTOUR PLOUGHING — ploughing along the contour lines (rather than up and down the slope) decelerates water flow and reduces erosion on slopes. (ii) TERRACE CULTIVATION — cutting steps on hill slopes turns them into level fields; widely practised in the western and central Himalayas; restricts erosion. (iii) STRIP CROPPING — large fields are divided into strips, with strips of grass left between strips of crop; the grass breaks the force of wind and water. (iv) SHELTER BELTS — rows of trees planted along the edges of fields slow down wind and have stabilised sand dunes in western India. (v) AFFORESTATION + proper grazing management. (vi) Control of mining; proper treatment and disposal of industrial effluents. Together these methods conserve topsoil, retain moisture and keep the land productive.

questions.question: Why is resource conservation essential for sustainable development? Discuss with reference to the Earth Summit and at least two specific challenges India faces.
questions.answer: INDISCRIMINATE use of resources concentrates them in a few hands and creates inequality between 'haves' and 'have-nots'. It has led to global ecological crises — global warming, ozone depletion, pollution and land degradation. SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT (Brundtland) means development that meets present needs without compromising the needs of future generations. The 1992 EARTH SUMMIT in Rio brought 100+ heads of state together; they signed declarations on climate change, biological diversity and AGENDA 21 — a global plan to combat environmental damage and poverty. INDIAN CHALLENGES: (a) very uneven distribution — Jharkhand mineral-rich, Rajasthan solar-rich but water-poor, Arunachal Pradesh water-rich but infrastructure-poor — so RESOURCE PLANNING by survey + planning structure + national integration is essential. (b) LAND DEGRADATION (130 million ha) from mining (Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh), over-grazing (Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP) and over-irrigation (Punjab, Haryana, western UP) — addressed by afforestation, shelter belts, terrace farming, controlled mining. Conservation is therefore both an environmental imperative and a development necessity.
